summary: In multicast VPNs, customer multicast flows travel through tunnels in a provider network, advertised by BGP auto-discovery routes. This RFC adds wildcards so a single route can say that many customer flows share one tunnel.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of writing a sign for each car on a bus, you write one sign saying all these cars ride the bus.

questions: what are wildcards in mvpn auto-discovery routes
how to advertise many multicast flows in one tunnel
what is an s-pmsi a-d route
what does c-* mean in mvpn
subtitle: Wildcards let one BGP route tell a provider network that many customer multicast flows share a single tunnel.

tldr.problem: In multicast VPNs, each auto-discovery route could name only one customer flow, and there was no way to say a selective tunnel is the default for all flows.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lets the source, the group, or both be a wildcard, encoded as a zero-length field in the S-PMSI A-D route, and defines how routers match flows to wildcard routes.
tldr.outcome: A router can originate fewer routes and so improve control-plane scalability. The number of tunnels in the data plane is not reduced.

today: RFC 6625 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6514. It has itself been updated by RFC 7582, RFC 7900 and RFC 8534.

sections.title: The Problem: One Route per Flow
sections.content:
In a Multicast Virtual Private Network (MVPN), a customer's multicast traffic crosses a service provider's network inside tunnels. The base specifications (RFC 6513 and RFC 6514) define BGP auto-discovery routes that announce which tunnel carries which customer flow.

Those routes have two limits. A single route names one customer flow, so binding many flows to one tunnel needs one route per flow. And there is no way to say that a tunnel is the default for all customer flows, except when that tunnel is joined by all the provider edge routers of the MVPN.

RFC 6625 removes both limits by allowing wildcard elements in the flow identifier. The extensions are OPTIONAL. It updates RFC 6514.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, you needed one label for every single passenger. Now one label can say "everyone" or "everyone going to this stop".

sections.title: Flows, Tunnels and Routes
sections.content:
Addresses in the customer's address space get the prefix C-, and addresses in the provider's get P-. A customer flow, or C-flow, is a pair (C-S,C-G) of a source address and a group address.

  • A P-tunnel is a tunnel through one or more service providers' networks.
  • An inclusive P-tunnel is joined by all PE routers attached to sites of the MVPN. A selective P-tunnel is joined only by PE routers that need to receive one of the flows on it.
  • An S-PMSI A-D route (Selective Provider Multicast Service Interface Auto-Discovery route) is carried in BGP Update messages and says which C-flows are bound to which P-tunnels.

The flow identifier goes in the route's NLRI, and the tunnel is named in an attribute called the PMSI Tunnel Attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is one TV channel from one sender. A tunnel is a pipe through the provider's network, and the route is the note saying which channels go in which pipe.

sections.title: Use Cases for Wildcards
sections.content:
A wildcard is written C-* and can replace the source, the group, or both, giving three kinds: (C-*,C-*), (C-S,C-*) and (C-*,C-G). The RFC lists several uses:

  • Using a selective P-tunnel as the default tunnel, by advertising (C-*,C-*).
  • Binding all flows on a customer's PIM-SM shared tree to one P-tunnel with (C-*,C-G), which applies only when the group is a non-bidirectional ASM group.
  • Binding flows with the same group address to one P-tunnel, even if they travel on source trees, or when they travel on a BIDIR-PIM shared tree.
  • Binding flows from one source to one P-tunnel regardless of group, which is useful for SSM addresses where a source sends several "channels".

A specific (C-S,C-G) can always be assigned individually. The RFC notes the benefit is control-plane scalability, with no effect on data-plane scalability since the number of P-tunnels is not reduced. Only unidirectional (point-to-multipoint) P-tunnels are covered.
sections.plainLanguage: You can write one note for all channels, all channels from one sender, or all senders of one channel, instead of a note per channel.

sections.title: How a Wildcard Is Encoded
sections.content:
The MCAST-VPN NLRI of an S-PMSI A-D route (from RFC 6514) holds an 8-octet RD, a one-octet multicast source length, the multicast source, a one-octet multicast group length, the multicast group, and the originating router's IP address. Before this RFC the two length fields always had a non-zero value.

RFC 6625 gives a zero length a meaning. A source wildcard is a source length of 0x00 with the source field omitted. A group wildcard is a group length of 0x00 with the group field omitted. A wildcard refers only to flows of the same address family (IPv4 or IPv6) as the route.
sections.plainLanguage: To say "anything", you leave that part of the label empty and write a zero where its length would go.

sections.title: Finding the Matching Route
sections.content:
Several routes may fit one flow, so the RFC gives an ordered match rule. For a flow (C-S,C-G) that a PE must transmit, it matches the first of these that the PE has currently originated:

  1. a route for (C-S,C-G);
  2. a route for (C-S,C-*), if C-G is an SSM group address;
  3. a route for (C-*,C-G), if C-G is an ASM group address;
  4. a route for (C-*,C-*).

A receiving PE applies the same order, but uses installed routes originated by its chosen upstream PE. The result does not depend on the order in which routes arrived, and can change as routes are withdrawn or new ones are advertised. For (C-*,C-G) traffic, extra conditions apply, such as the upstream PE being the one for the customer rendezvous point, or the group being a BIDIR-PIM group.
sections.plainLanguage: You look for the most specific sign first, and fall back to the more general ones if you do not find it.

sections.title: Procedures for Each Kind of Wildcard
sections.content:
Originating a given kind of wildcard route is OPTIONAL. But a PE that can originate a kind MUST be able to process it, and SHOULD be able to process all three. A PE MUST NOT originate a kind unless it is known a priori that all PEs attached to the MVPN can process it. The criteria for originating and withdrawing are local to the originating PE.

  • (C-*,C-G): used only when C-G is an ASM group address. A receiver that can tell the group is SSM SHOULD "ignore" the route.
  • (C-S,C-*): used only for flows whose group is an SSM address. A receiver that can tell otherwise SHOULD "ignore" it.
  • (C-*,C-*): used when a PE has a policy not to use an inclusive tunnel for the MVPN. With BGP C-multicast routing this gives the "S-PMSI only" model with no I-PMSIs at all.

For each kind, an implementation MUST allow the Route Targets to be set by configuration, and otherwise the route MUST carry the default set. If a PE transmits a flow that matches a wildcard route, it MUST use that route's P-tunnel. If PIM is the PE-PE protocol, a PE with matching state MUST join the advertised P-tunnel. Here "ignored" means only that the route is not considered when choosing a tunnel for receiving data, not that normal BGP processing is skipped.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the group must understand a kind of sign before anyone uses it, and each sign only makes sense for the right kind of channel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that there are no additional security considerations beyond those of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, the base MVPN specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Wildcards do not add any new safety worries beyond the ones the older rules already had.
